games.explanation: Wheeler is the better pitcher, nobody's arguing that, but a plus-money dog against him should exist somewhere in the two-to-one range and this one is closer to a coin flip than the board wants to admit. Toronto's top three punish right-handed pitching as a group, and Guerrero in particular has been a different animal this year with a wOBA north of .400. Soriano's walks are a real problem, but a hot ballpark with the wind blowing across turns any Springer or Vlad contact into a scoring event, and the sim has this within half a run. At +193 you don't need Toronto to be the better team, you just need them to be live, and they are.

The market is treating this like a coin flip because Washington is at home, but the pitching matchup is doing all the work in the other direction. Cade Cavalli has been a very different arm depending on who's in the box, and against righties he's been walking the ballpark while giving up loud contact at a nearly 49% hard-hit clip. That happens to be exactly the wheelhouse for a Reds top of the order stacked with right-handed thump, with Elly and Sal Stewart in particular built to punish the pitch profile Cavalli survives on. Getting plus money on the better team, against the more vulnerable starter, is the entire argument.

Fried has been quietly leaking value all year against right-handed bats, which is inconvenient when the lineup across the diamond is stacked with them. Acuña has been a different hitter versus righties than lefties and Olson is right there with him, so the platoon Fried usually leans on to survive isn't available tonight. Mahle isn't a star but he doesn't need to be in a park where the ball travels and the wind is doing nothing to help either staff. Getting a road dog price on the Elo favorite is the kind of math you take every time, and +137 on a team the market has priced as an underdog is the whole ballgame.

Nobody wants to back the White Sox on the road, which is exactly why the price got this fat. Cleveland is trotting out a soft-tossing lefty rookie whose numbers against righties are considerably more human than his overall line, and Chicago happens to run out a lineup full of them. Grichuk in particular is the kind of right-handed bat that eats this profile alive, and the sim has this game landing inside a run either way. At +130, you're getting plus money on a coin flip the market has quietly turned into a laugher.

Eovaldi's surface numbers scream ace, but the board is treating Baltimore like they showed up to lose, and that's the mistake. The Orioles happen to run out a top of the order stacked with lefty bats, which is exactly where Eovaldi's edge quietly disappears, and Pete Alonso against right-handed pitching is one of the more punishing at-bats in the sport at a .403 xwOBA. Shane Baz walks too many hitters to be lovable, but the sim still lands on a dead-even 4.6 to 4.6 game, which is not what +137 is pricing. When the projected score is a coin flip and the number is plus money, you take the plus money.

Sasaki is being priced like a phenom and pitching like a walk machine, and the Diamondbacks happen to run a lineup built to punish exactly that. He's issuing free passes to nearly 14% of the hitters he sees and getting barreled up when he's forced into the zone, which is a rough combination against a Carroll-Perdomo top of the order that gets on base for a living. Merrill Kelly is the steadier arm in this game by a wide margin, and the roof-closed environment neutralizes the one thing Dodger power hitters actually need. At +162 on a coin flip our sim has closer to 57%, the underdog price is doing the heavy lifting.
